newsitem.title: UK: LME plan to alter constitution likely to be adopted.
newsitem.headline: LME plan to alter constitution likely to be adopted.

text.p: Members of the London Metal Exchange (LME) are expected to approve changes to the market's constitution at a special meeting next week - another step in implementing reforms prompted by 1996's Sumitomo Corp scandal.
On Monday the LME holds an Extraordinary Ordinary General Meeting (EGM) to specifically approve amending its Articles of Association.
The main thrust of the proposals is to increase the size of the LME Board by extending the number of directors that are not associated with ring-dealing or non-ring dealing companies.

Specifically, the Board size would be increasaed by two with invited directors to number six instead of four. The Board's other constituents would remain the same at eight directors from ring-dealing firms, three from non ring-dealer companies and the Chief Executive.
This will alter the balance of power on the Board, as the six invited directors and the three non-ring directors could, in theory, out-vote the eight ring-dealers.

The proposals are expected to be adopted, as they follow on from last December's Securities and Investments Board (SIB) review of the LME. Members can vote by post, by proxy, or turn up at the EGM which will be in the LME's Board room.
These amendments have aroused differing views among LME members as some senior sources with ring-dealing companies are unhappy at the probable dilution of their influence on the Board.
Although ring-dealing company numbers have fallen in recent years to 16 out of a total LME membership of around 100, they still account for 70 percent of the LME's cleared business.
The bulk of the LME's liquidity and price discovery functions are being provided by ring-dealing companies who have to absorb greater costs.
"The average team now (on the floor) is around 12 people - that is double ten years ago," one said.
However, sources at non-ring dealing companies - increasingly influential in the downstream metals business now - feel that these measures do not go far enough.
"This does nothing to redress the inbalance between the ring-dealing and the non-dealing firms. There will still be just three directors representing us," a director at one company said.
The make-up of the LME Board was one of the areas highlighted by the SIB in the review of the metal market it carried out after the Sumitomo scandal.
Last June the Japanese company reported losses of $2.6 billion in unauthorised copper trades allegedly carried out by its former head trader Yasuo Hamanaka.
In its review SIB said there was support for the view that the Board's composition should better represent the whole membership, with more directors having no association with the metals industry.
The LME is currently implementing the SIB's overall proposals, which also encompass warehousing, transparency, information sharing, the overall role of the Board and the Exchange's Executive.
